title: 我曾把自己的影子叫作恶魔 / I Used to Call My Shadow a Demon
body:
中文版

我曾把自己的影子叫作恶魔

小时候，我一直觉得身体里住着一个恶魔。

它没有声音，也没有模样。可每当我想走向别人，它就会拉住我。课间的笑声隔着几步远，我却不知道该在什么时候开口。好不容易说出一句话，又会在晚上反复回想：是不是说错了？他们会不会觉得我很奇怪？

那时的我不懂得解释这些感受，只觉得自己像被什么附身了。别人似乎天生就会相处，而我连一句简单的问候，都要在心里排练许多遍。

后来，我学会观察别人的表情，猜测每一次沉默。我把自己的喜好藏起来，努力成为一个好相处的人。有人喜欢热闹，我就跟着笑；有人讨厌某件事，我便赶紧收起自己的兴趣。可是越努力，我越不知道该怎样自然地站在人群里。

一次普通的冷场，也能让我怀疑自己很久。我常想，如果能换一种性格，是不是生活就会轻松一些？

有一天，整理旧物时，我翻到小时候的画。纸上的线条歪歪扭扭，有些颜色甚至涂出了边界。我记得画它们的时候，自己很快乐。那时我还没有学会事事询问别人的眼光。

我坐在地上，看了很久。

原来，在那些笨拙的交谈、退缩的脚步和漫长的沉默之外，我也有喜欢的事，有想表达的东西。我可以用很长时间画一张画，可以留意傍晚窗边的颜色，也会因为别人一句无意的话难过。这些都是我。

从那以后，我试着一点点了解自己。什么时候需要独处，什么样的相处让我舒服，哪些答应只是因为害怕被讨厌。我仍然会紧张，仍然偶尔说错话，但开始允许一句话说完以后，就留在那个下午。

童年那个被我叫作恶魔的影子，也渐渐有了别的名字：害怕、敏感，还有想被接纳的愿望。

我终于愿意坐到它身边。

认识自己并没有让我立刻变得擅长交往。只是下一次站在人群外时，我不再急着责怪自己。我可以先打一个招呼，也可以慢一点，找到愿意听我把话说完的人。

回家的路上，路灯把影子拉得很长。

我看见它跟着我的脚步，一起往前走。

────────────────────

English Version

I Used to Call My Shadow a Demon

As a child, I believed a demon lived inside me.

It had neither a voice nor a face. But whenever I wanted to approach someone, it seemed to hold me back. At school, laughter was only a few steps away, yet I never knew when to join in. If I finally managed to say something, I would replay it that night. Had it sounded wrong? Did they think I was strange?

I had no language for those feelings. Being possessed was the closest explanation I could imagine. Other children seemed to know instinctively how to get along. I rehearsed even the simplest greeting.

As I grew older, I learned to study expressions and search for meaning in every silence. I hid my preferences and tried to become easy to like. When people wanted noise, I laughed along. When they dismissed something I enjoyed, I quietly put it away. The harder I tried, the less I knew how to be myself around anyone.

An ordinary pause in a conversation could leave me questioning myself for days. I wondered whether life would be easier with a different personality.

One afternoon, while sorting through old belongings, I found drawings I had made as a child. The lines were crooked. Some of the colours spilled beyond their borders. I remembered how happy I had been making them, before I learned to consult an imaginary audience about everything I did.

I sat on the floor and looked at them for a long time.

Beyond the awkward conversations and hesitant footsteps, I had interests of my own. I could spend hours on a drawing. I noticed the changing colours beside a window at dusk. A careless remark could hurt me deeply. All of these things belonged to the same person.

Gradually, I began to pay attention. When did I need time alone? Which friendships felt comfortable? How often did I say yes because I was afraid of being disliked?

I still grew nervous. I still said the wrong thing sometimes. But I began to let a conversation stay in the afternoon where it had happened.

The shadow I had called a demon slowly acquired other names: fear, sensitivity, the wish to belong.

Eventually, I was willing to sit beside it.

Understanding myself did not suddenly make conversation easy. But the next time I stood outside a group, I felt less need to blame myself. I could offer a greeting. I could take my time and find someone willing to hear me finish a sentence.

On the walk home, a streetlight stretched my shadow across the pavement.

I watched it follow my footsteps as we moved forward.
